episodes.215547: As a storm system and cold front moved through Middle Tennessee on August 22, 2026, scattered thunderstorms developed, especially across the Cumberland Plateau. Abundant instability and forcing from the front caused these thunderstorms to become severe. Several reports of downed trees and large hail of 1 to 1.5 inches were received.

episodes.215778: Storms along and behind a warm frontal passage began to form in an environment with ample instability, moisture, and shear during the evening hours of August 22, 2026. These storms initially began to exhibit upscale growth across western Pennsylvania, producing large hail in Elk County as that specific storm moved north-northeastward into McKean County and produced an isolated instance of tree damage. Further south, a line of thunderstorms spanning across Clearfield and Cambria Counties shifted further eastward with embedded circulations beginning to form. One of these circulations produced an EF-1 tornado in Madera before lifting and producing straight-line wind damage closer to Clearfield-Centre County line. This storm continued to produce isolated wind damage further eastward into Centre County. Across southern Pennsylvania, slow-moving severe thunderstorms produced multiple instances of flash flooding in Somerset and Bedford County with isolated wind damage across Bedford, Fulton, and Franklin Counties.
episodes.215807: Three rounds of thunderstorm activity occurred from late on August 20 through the evening of August 22. One decaying MCS crossed into northeastern Central Alabama early on August 21, causing scattered tree damage across Cherokee, Etowah, and St. Clair counties. Scattered activity occurred during the evening of the 21st, including in Barbour, Marengo, and Tallapoosa counties. The third round came on the evening of the 22nd, with another MCS moving down the I-22 corridor through Marion, Fayette, and Walker counties, weakening below severe limits before reaching the Birmingham metro area.
episodes.216248: The potential for strong to severe thunderstorms grew in earnest on the afternoon of August 22nd across northeast Kentucky in response to an approaching cold front. The area escaped from seeing much in the way of storm damage, with the exception of a singular instance of a downed tree and power line in South Shore. Otherwise, the frontal boundary completed its passage that evening and brought the severe threat to an end in northeast Kentucky.
episodes.216249: August proved to be a very active weather month as daily chances of showers and storms stretched into the 22nd and 23rd. The culprit behind this timeframe of storms came in the form of a warm front shifting just north of the area on the 22nd and a cold front approaching from the west. This front arrived during the evening, then progressed east across the area overnight. ||Showers and storms accompanying these fronts produced one to two inches of rain across ports of southeast Ohio. Heavier rainfall amounts upstream led to flooding on West Fork Duck Creek at Macksburg. Damaging winds also accompanying these storms resulted in a cluster of tree and power line damage noted across much of southeast Ohio before the front's departure to the south late on August 23rd. In the town of Wellston, multiple downed trees fell down into nearby homes. The risk for thunderstorms quickly came to an end once the frontal boundary completed its passage through southeast Ohio.
episodes.216250: Active weather continued to stretch into the second half of August across West Virginia under the guise of a warm front and cold front combination sweeping through the region. A swath of tree and power line damage was noted across north-central West Virginia on the afternoon of August 22nd while warm and unstable conditions thrived ahead of the frontal passage. The front completed its journey through the area by late in the day, bringing the severe threat to an end.
episodes.216363: A severe thunderstorm traveled south out of Nebraska and produced strong winds across northeast Weld and northern Logan Counties, with the strongest measured wind gust reaching 71 mph.
episodes.216365: During the afternoon of August 22, a thunderstorm developed over southeast Weld county along an outflow boundary. This storm quickly intensified as it moved northeast and approached I-76 near the Weld/Morgan county line, where it produced a significant swath of damage from Empire Reservoir through Jackson Lake State Park. A storm survey was conducted on August 25, which revealed a swath of significant straight line wind and wind-driven hail damage along a 11 mile path. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 80 mph, along with a maximum hail size of approximately 2 inches in diameter.||In addition to this storm, a severe thunderstorm dropped 1.5 inch diameter hail and produce wind gusts up to 67 mph across western Arapahoe County. A third severe thunderstorms also brought hail up to 1.25 inch in diameter to the Brighton and Fort Lupton area.

episodes.217726: A broad sub-tropical ridge axis was centered to the west of the area over Texas and the southern Plains resulting in a deep layer northerly flow regime in the mid and upper levels of the atmosphere.  Additionally, a weak mid-level trough axis extended east-southeastward from central Louisiana toward Lower Alabama.   A mesoscale convective complex of strong to severe thunderstorms developed along the mid-level boundary over central Mississippi and then swept southward through southeast Louisiana and southern Mississippi during the afternoon and early evening hours.  The severe storms within the larger convective complex produced severe wind gusts and hail in the region.
episodes.217728: A broad sub-tropical ridge axis was centered to the west of the area over Texas and the southern Plains resulting in a deep layer northerly flow regime in the mid and upper levels of the atmosphere. Additionally, a weak mid-level trough axis extended east-southeastward from central Louisiana toward Lower Alabama. A mesoscale convective complex of strong to severe thunderstorms developed along the mid-level boundary over central Mississippi and then swept southward through portions of the coastal waters in the late afternoon and early evening hours. The severe storms within the larger convective complex produced severe marine thunderstorm wind gusts in Lake Pontchartrain and the Gulf waters off the coast of Louisiana.
episodes.217823: On August 18th, weak shortwave energy moved through the eastern periphery of the Heat Wave ridge over a moist and unstable airmass enhancing storms mainly over northeast and central Florida. Scattered showers and storms developed along the inland-moving sea breezes with stronger storms, capable of wet microbursts, pulsing along mesoscale boundary collisions in the afternoon into evening. On August 19-20, a frontal boundary stalled over southern Georgia as ���Heat Wave��� ridging built in from the west. Tropical moisture of 2+ inches of precipitable water remained south of the front, mainly over northeast Florida. Scattered showers and storms developed along the inland-moving sea breezes. The combination of high moisture, strong diurnal heating, and sea breeze/outflow interactions supported strong to severe storms capable of producing damaging winds, frequent lightning strikes and torrential downpours. Weak steering flow allowed for localized flooding. On August 22nd, lingering upper shortwaves ahead of the weakening frontal boundary in central Georgia triggered morning showers and isolated storms moving inland from the Gulf. Convection then spread east-northeastward through the day in the general southwest flow. A few stronger storms occurred along sea breeze boundary mergers in the late morning to early afternoon hours in north-central Florida.
episodes.217858: A shortwave trough moved across the northern rockies, causing the high pressure to shift back westward. Deep monsoonal moisture in place and the forcing from this shortwave trough resulted in thunderstorm development with heavy rainfall causing flash flooding and debris flows mainly impacting the burn scar areas, particularly the Gold Mountain Burn Scar and Lee Burn Scar. Storms training over the Lee Burn Scar in particular resulted in debris flows and mudslides both on the 23rd and 24th of August.
episodes.217882: An MCS began to track southeast from eastern Kansas during the morning of August 22nd. Model soundings across the Mid-South depicted an inverted-V with mid-level lapse rates around 7.0 C/km. By the afternoon hours, a large bow began to race across the Mid-South with a large swath of damaging winds in its path.
episodes.217883: High amplitude upper level ridging began shifting east of the region late on the 21st into the 22nd. This allowed for a deep southerly flow aloft to advect in monsoonal moisture, which resulted in two days of strong to severe thunderstorms across the region. Forecast soundings for the 22nd were not overly supportive of widespread strong wind gusts (Modestly deep inverted-V profile), with only one observation reaching severe criteria. A cold front approaching the area on the 23rd maximized warm air advection and allowed for numerous thunderstorms to develop in the warm sector. The main concern with the setup was for sub-optimal kinematics - thermodynamics and forcing were both more than sufficient. Quite a few severe gusts were observed on the 23rd, making it the much more active day compared to the 22nd.
episodes.217925: A severe thunderstorm complex tracked across northwest Montana, producing strong winds, heavy rain, and power outages.

episodes.218168: Low pressure moved through the Great Lakes region on the afternoon of August 22nd dragging a cold front through the area that evening. Ahead of the cold front, a pre-frontal trough crossed through the region providing forcing for severe thunderstorms. The environment had uncapped instability of 1000-2000 J/kg of MLCAPE with steep low level lapse rates of around 8 C/km and DCAPE of 500-800. In addition, there was deep layer shear of 20-30 knots supporting damaging winds and isolated large hail.
episodes.218176: A cold front crossed Lake Erie during the afternoon and early evening hours on August 22. Rounds of thunderstorms occurred across parts of the lake along and ahead of the front, with one round occurring during the overnight and early morning hours on the 22nd and a second round occurring during the afternoon. Some of these thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts over the lake.
episodes.218227: A heat wave developed across the region during late August. A weak boundary and short wave approached from the north causing strong to severe storms.
episodes.218234: A strong dust devil developed behind a church in Buna damaging the soffit and roof.
episodes.218240: During the afternoon and early evening hours of August 22nd, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along a weak cold front as it was moving through central Kentucky. Daytime heating allowed temperatures to rise into the 80s, with dew points in the upper 60s to low 70s ahead of the front, allowing for about 2000-2500 J/kg of MLCAPE. With the nose of a 40-50 kt 500 mb jet overhead, the stronger flow helped result in 25-30 kt of deep-layer shear. While limited moisture aloft helped keep most convection sub-severe, a small cluster of storms that developed in north central Kentucky produced severe winds and hail, including a 73 mph wind gust at the Cumberland County Mesonet station.
episodes.218259: During the very early morning of August 22nd, a broken line of thunderstorms dove due south through south-central Illinois. In Madison, Marion, and Clinton counties, hailstones of 1 to 2.5 inches were reported.
episodes.218296: A warm and moist airmass was in place across the region on August 22. Isolated to scattered slow-moving storms resulted in flash flooding near Norfolk and across the VA Eastern Shore.

This storm quickly intensified as it moved northeast and approached I-76 near the Weld/Morgan county line, where it produced a significant swath of damage from Empire Reservoir through Jackson Lake State Park. A storm survey was conducted on August 25, which revealed a swath of significant straight line wind and wind-driven hail damage along a 11 mile path. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 80 mph, along with a maximum hail size of approximately 2 inches in |diameter.||Damage was first evident on the northwest side of Empire Reservoir along Highway 34. Significant crop loss was noted in many fields, along with complete defoliation of vegetation along and north of the South Platte River. Most residences along a roughly 3 mile stretch of Highway 34 were damaged, with most south and west facing windows broken, along with substantial damage to vinyl siding. The combination of wind and hail also injured horses and killed two calves at one residence. ||Damage continued into far western Morgan county, including the town of Orchard, where an estimated 60 percent of homes had broken windows and/or siding damage. More severe damage was also evident just to the west and northwest of the town, where several trees were uprooted and a few houses had almost all of the siding on|west-facing walls removed from the combination of wind and hail. A large carport at a residence to the southwest of Jackson Lake State Park was lifted over the house, with some of this debris thrown about 50 yards to the northeast. Within the State Park,|several trees were uprooted, and two minor injuries were reported from hail. The combination of wind and hail also damaged nearly every vehicle and camper in the area.

An EF-1 tornado occurred during the evening hours of August 22, 2026 as a line of thunderstorms merged with a supercell thunderstorm and produced a tornado in the town of Madera. The tornadic damage began on Belsena Road near Elm Street, where a large tree was blown across the road. Multiple trees were uprooted or snapped and a roof was torn off of a residence on Spruce Street. Trees were also snapped and uprooted on the east side of Madera on Alexander Road and Heritage Lane. The tornado  was on the ground for approximately 2 minutes and traveled approximately 1 mile before dissipating. Straight line winds continued to produce sporadic damage to the northeast of Madera. Maximum estimated wind speeds of this tornado were 90 mph with a maximum path width of 150 yards.
